. As Savransky (2021: 4) observes: ‘the End of the World is always the end of some world in this world [. . .] the Euro-American extractive mode of living through which “civilization developed,” is not the end of everything as such’.

Accordingly, sociologists should understand that futurelessness is always the foreclosing of some futures among other possible futures in this world, and we need always to ask for whom are those futures foreclosing and how is this made to matter. I have addressed a particular European (or perhaps Euro-North American) kind of futurelessness expressed by writers on the political left. But, as Mitchell and Chaudhury (2020: 322) show, there are other futures available, which they explore through Afrofuturist, Desi-futures and myriad other non-European futurisms that ‘open space for futures beyond (the) apocalypse (of whiteness)’.
